av_event.line_text: Yeah, that's exactly what my dad says. Word for word, pretty much. I do worry about him, I'll be honest.
av_event.what: Callum glances down at the table and lets out a slow breath, pausing for about a second before saying 'I do worry about him', his half-smile dropping briefly before it comes back.

text:
A: Hello, love! Ooh, it's you. I said you looked lovely in your photo. I'm Debbie.
B: Ha, thank you. Hiya, Debbie, I'm Callum. You alright?
A: I'm fine, love, thank you. Bit worn out with all this talking, I'm not used to it. Where are you, then?
B: Sittingbourne, in Kent. Whereabouts are you?
A: Gorleston-on-Sea. Right by Great Yarmouth.
B: Oh, no way, we come up to Norfolk most summers, me and my wife. Caravan or a cottage. We did one near Hemsby a couple of years back.
A: Hemsby! That's just up the road, love. Did you get fish and chips on the front?
B: Pretty much every night. Megan was like, we can't have chips again, and then we had chips again.
A: That's what you're supposed to do on holiday, that is. We have them every Friday, me and my husband Steve, and we live here.
B: Ha. Fair enough. Did you get on alright with the puzzle at the start?
A: Oh, don't. The dog started barking halfway through and I lost my place. What do you do, love?
B: I'm a machine operator. I run a printer-folder-gluer at a cardboard box factory. The board goes in flat and comes out a box, basically.
A: Oh, I did packing for years! Frozen food, near Yarmouth. I bet I've packed things into your boxes.
B: Could've done, actually. We do a lot of food stuff, outer cases mostly.
A: I always liked it, you know, getting into a rhythm on the line, and the girls were lovely. I just couldn't be doing with the forms. I nearly got written up once for forgetting my hairnet three days running.
B: Three days! Our lot would've had you in for a chat.
A: Well, I left about two years ago anyway. They changed the shifts, and I mind my grandson now. Do you like your shifts?
B: Erm, mostly. Days one week, backs the next. You're knackered by the end of a run of backs, but you get used to it. I'd like to go for shift team leader in a couple of years, maybe.
A: Ooh, good for you. I never wanted to, too much hassle, too many forms. But you'd be good at it, you seem ever so calm.
B: Thank you. Yeah, I try not to get rattled. My dad's the same. He drives for a haulage firm, has done for years, but his back's bad now from all that time in the cab, you know.
A: Oh, that's my Steve with his knees. He does removals with his van, and I keep saying to him, you can't be lugging wardrobes at sixty-one forever. He just says, well, who else is going to do it?
B: Yeah, that's exactly what my dad says. Word for word, pretty much. I do worry about him, I'll be honest.
A: Course you do, love. That's because you're a good son. My boy's a bit older than you, and you've got the same smile, you have.
B: Aw, that's nice. Does he live near you?
A: Ten minutes away. They all do, the whole lot of them. Sorry, I've gone off on one again, I always do. What do you do for fun?
B: Five-a-side on Wednesdays, and the garden. I've got tomatoes going, but half of them are still green, so I don't know if they'll make it.
A: Put them in a drawer with a banana, love. That's what my mum always did. Brings them on lovely, that does.
B: A banana? Really? Hira said the windowsill, but our cat knocks everything off the windowsill, so a drawer might be the answer.
A: There you go! Out of reach of the cat and all. Do you follow the football? Steve and my son are Norwich mad.
B: Gillingham, with my dad. Bit of a rough season, so don't ask.
A: Oh, Norwich are the same, love. Steve shouts at the radio every Saturday, and I just put the kettle on and-
